about: An enumeration of what an A1 Hindi candidate must be able to do, restated in the project's own words. It is NOT sourced from a Hindi awarding body and must not be read as one. core/exam-levels.json maps Hindi A1 to the Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha 'Prathmic' rung with basis 'editorial' -- the project's judgement, not a published alignment -- and that judgement was re-checked before this file was written. DBHPS publishes the NAMES of its examinations (Parichaya, Prathamic, Madhyama, Rashtrabhasha, Praveshika, Rashtrabhasha Visharad, Rashtrabhasha Praveen) and the prescribed readers for each, but no content syllabus: no grammar inventory, no word list, no can-do descriptors, and no A1/A2 split. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO DBHPS. Kendriya Hindi Sansthan and the Central Hindi Training Institute were checked for the same and publish no public level-split content inventory either, and no Council of Europe Reference Level Description exists for Hindi. Two things therefore bound this enumeration, and `scope` names which of them bounds each dimension: (1) the CEFR Companion Volume's published A1 descriptors, which are finite and level-split but language-neutral, so every Hindi exponent chosen to realise a descriptor is the project's choice and not the Council's; and (2) the project's own checked-in Hindi A1 contract -- hindi/assessment-spec.md, hindi/task-shapes/a1.json, and the two timed mocks in hindi/mocks/a1/ -- which IS finite, IS specific to Hindi, and IS what a learner is actually scored against, but which this project wrote itself. Every point here is consequently editorial. The strongest claims in the file are the ones whose `note` cites a numbered item in a checked-in A1 mock: for those the demand is written down and dated rather than inferred, and a reader can check the claim against the mock in one step. Every scope dimension is `partial`, this inventory is NOT complete, and the coverage percentage it produces is a measure of the corpus against this list -- never an exam-readiness claim.
source: No awarding-body content syllabus exists for Hindi A1; see `about`. The bounding sources are the project's own checked-in A1 contract at https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/hindi/assessment-spec.md and the Council of Europe CEFR Companion Volume A1 descriptors at https://www.coe.int/en/web/common-european-framework-reference-languages/cefr-companion-volume-and-its-language-versions. The DBHPS pages that were checked and found to publish exam names but no syllabus are https://www.dbhpscentral.org/Syllabus.html and https://dbhpscentral.org/examination.html (checked 2026-09-01).

communicative-functions.note: The CEFR Companion Volume's A1 column IS finite and level-split, which is what closes a dimension, but it is language-neutral: it says a candidate can 'ask and answer questions about personal details' and never says which Hindi words do that. The forty points here pair each A1 descriptor the level implies with the exponent this project would accept, and the exponent is always our choice. Where a checked-in A1 mock item pins the exponent down -- the cafe price turn, the sign-reading items, the named-reader message -- the point's note cites the item. This dimension closes when a Hindi-specific functional inventory with published exponents exists, or when the project declares its own mock set the definitive A1 function list and freezes it.

grammar.note: THE HARDEST DIMENSION TO SOURCE, AND THE REASON THIS FILE IS PARTIAL RATHER THAN COMPLETE. There is no published Hindi equivalent of the PCIC grammar inventory or the Goethe word list -- nothing that enumerates Hindi constructions and marks them A1 or A2. The grammar points here were derived the only defensible way available: by reading every stimulus in the two checked-in A1 mocks and enumerating the construction each one requires, then adding the constructions those constructions presuppose. That yields a floor, not a closure -- a construction absent from both mocks is absent from this list too, however ordinary it is. Treat a covered grammar point as 'the track teaches what these two mocks demand of it', never as 'the track teaches A1 Hindi grammar'.

phonology-orthography.source: The Unicode Devanagari block (U+0900-U+097F) for the inventory of letters, and https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/hindi/pronunciation-reference.md
phonology-orthography.note: The written half is nearly closed and the spoken half is not, which is the same shape the Spanish inventory records. Devanagari's letter inventory IS finite and enumerable, so the script points can state exactly which letters the track has an atom for and which it does not; that is a real boundary and the notes give the counts. Pronunciation has no such boundary: no source separates A1 Hindi phonology from A2, so contrasts, stress and intonation are enumerated here on the project's judgement and left honestly unmapped where nothing teaches them. Drawing the A1/A2 pronunciation line ourselves would be the editorial promotion the Spanish file declines to make, so this dimension stays partial for the same stated reason.

lexicon.source: https://github.com/adhithyan15/coding-adventures/blob/main/code/learning/human-languages/hindi/mocks/a1/ and the topic areas named in hindi/assessment-spec.md
lexicon.note: No published A1 Hindi word list exists -- no DBHPS list, no Goethe-style Wortliste, no ranked frequency band adopted by any Hindi awarding body. What is enumerated here is twenty-five DOMAINS, bounded by the topics the checked-in A1 mocks and assessment spec actually test, with a probe naming representative headwords the track would need in each. A domain point is therefore a claim that the track has a usable foothold in that domain, not that it holds the domain's full A1 vocabulary. No per-word count is claimed complete and none should be inferred: this file deliberately contains no 'holds N headwords' point, because a probe cannot honestly express one.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding -- an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped. Every atom named in every probe in this file was checked against the atoms the hindi track actually introduces at the time of writing; a probe naming an atom that does not exist would report 'not covered' forever and be indistinguishable from real debt, so an id was never invented to fill a point. A point the corpus cannot demonstrate gets `probe: null` and a note saying what is missing and, wherever the demand is written down, which checked-in A1 mock item makes it.

points.label: proper nouns: personal names, used in address and written into a form field
grammatical gender is inherent: the -a/-i lean helps and then fails, so gender is learned with the word
gender by heteronymy for people: pita/mata, bhai/bahin, beta/beti
number: forming the plural of a masculine -a noun, a feminine -i noun, and a consonant-final noun
points.note: No atom teaches plural morphology. The corpus introduces log ('people') as a lexical item and nothing else. Both checked-in A1 mocks require a plural read (mock 1 item 16 and mock 2 item 20 both turn on 'do bhashaen bolti hai'), so this is a demand the level makes and the track does not meet.

points.label: the oblique form a noun takes before a postposition (larka -> larke ko)
points.note: The corpus teaches me (in) and the ka/ke genitive, but never the case change the noun in front of them undergoes. Nothing to probe.

points.label: a numeral stands in front of the noun it counts (ek chay)
first-person singular main
second person: choosing between respectful ap and familiar tum
third person / demonstrative yah and vah
first-person plural ham
points.note: ham appears only as a substring inside mehman in the corpus's headwords; no lesson introduces it. Mock 2 reading item 10 ('ham station par milenge') requires it.

points.label: possessive mera, and its agreement mera / meri / mere with the thing owned
possessive apka for the respectful addressee
the oblique first person mujhe, when the sentence will not let you be its subject
the other oblique pronouns: apko, use, hamen, tumhen
points.note: Only mujhe is introduced, and it is introduced as part of the pasand frame rather than as a paradigm. Nothing probes the rest of the series.

points.label: the y- / v- / k- system: one stem set gives near, far and interrogative
an attributive adjective stands in front of its noun
-a adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number
invariable adjectives that never change shape (lal, safed, thik)
predicative use: an adjective plus the copula (main thik hun)
degree: kam and zyada as everyday quantifiers
thoda as a hedging quantifier ('a little')
points.note: Mock 1 listening item 12 keys on 'han, thodi'. No lesson introduces thoda/thodi.

points.label: comparison with se (X Y se bara hai)
points.note: Comparison needs the postposition se, which the corpus never introduces. See HI-A1-POST-04.

points.label: the -na infinitive names the verb and yields the stem
the present copula hona: hun, hai, hain
the copula with tum: ho
points.note: ho occurs inside the age frame ('tum kitne sal ke ho?') but no atom introduces the tum copula, so nothing demonstrates it independently of that one memorised question.

points.label: the present habitual: stem + -ta/-ti/-te + hona
the present habitual agrees twice: participle for gender and number, copula for person
negating a statement by putting nahin in front of the verb
the present continuous raha/rahi/rahe hai as a productive pattern
points.note: The continuous appears twice as a fixed frame -- 'ek baj raha hai' in the hour lesson and 'barish ho rahi hai' in the weather lesson -- but no atom presents it as a pattern that applies to any stem, the way the habitual lesson does for -ta.

points.label: recognising a future form in a set phrase (phir milenge)
forming the future productively: -unga / -ega / -engi and its agreement
points.note: Both mocks depend on it in the very first scored part: mock 1 reading item 8 ('main panch baje aunga'), item 11 ('bas das minat me aegi'), mock 2 item 8 and item 13. milenge is taught as one memorised farewell, not as a tense.

points.label: the past / perfective, and the ne construction that goes with it
points.note: Nothing in the corpus is past-tense. This is arguably outside a minimal A1 construct, but the level's own can-do descriptors include saying where one came from and reporting a completed everyday event, and neither mock avoids the ambiguity by design.

points.label: the polite -iye imperative used for requests (dijiye, kijiye)
the plain and familiar imperatives (bol, bolo, boliye as a series)
points.note: Only the -iye form is introduced, and only inside two fixed courtesy phrases. No atom presents the imperative as a paradigm.

points.label: the negative imperative with mat
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 3 is exactly this ('yahan mat baithiye'). The corpus introduces neither mat nor na as a prohibitive.

points.label: noun + karna compound verbs (kam karna, madad karna, pasand karna)
the experiencer frame: mujhe X pasand hai, where the liked thing is the subject
chahiye for wanting and needing
points.note: Mock 1 reading item 12 ('mujhe chay chahiye') and profile 2 ('use pani chahiye') both key on it; mock 2 listening item 9 does too. No lesson introduces chahiye.

points.label: sakna for ability and possibility (a sakte hain)
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 14 is 'kya ap kal a sakte hain?'. Nothing in the corpus introduces sakna.

points.label: jana, and the go-somewhere frame every A1 routine description needs
points.note: Neither jana nor its stem is introduced anywhere. Every personal-account item in both mocks uses it (kam par jati hun, train se kam par jata hai, bazar jata hun), and the A1 speaking interview asks about transport and routine. This is the single highest-traffic missing verb in the level.

points.label: khana and pina as verbs, distinguished from khana the noun
points.note: khana is introduced as the masculine noun 'food'. The verb sense, and pina at all, are untaught; mock 1's account has 'khana khati hun' and mock 2's has 'chay piti hai'.

points.label: postpositions follow their noun where English would put a preposition in front
me for location and containment
the genitive ka / ke / ki for possession and belonging
se for origin, instrument and means (Dilli se, bas se)
points.note: Load-bearing in both mocks: 'Aman Dilli se hai', 'Ravi bas se school jata hai', 'ap kahan se hain?', 'main Bhopal se hun', 'train se kam par jata hai'. The corpus never introduces se, and the A1 speaking interview's origin question cannot be answered without it.

points.label: par for location at a point (ghar par, station par)
points.note: Mock 1 reading item 14 and mock 2 item 10 both turn on it. Untaught.

points.label: ko as a free postposition marking an object or a recipient
points.note: Only the fused mujhe is present. ko itself is never introduced, so neither a marked object nor a dative recipient can be built.

points.label: ke sath for accompaniment
points.note: Mock 1's account has 'apne dost ke sath' and mock 2's has 'apne parivar ke sath'. Untaught.

points.label: spatial compound postpositions: ke pas, ke samne, ke piche
points.note: Mock 2 listening item 6 ('bas station ke samne hai') and item 11 ('nahin, pas hai') both need them. Untaught.

points.label: se ... tak for a span of days or hours
points.note: Mock 2's account opens 'somvar se shukravar tak'. The weekday nouns are taught; the frame that spans them is not.

points.label: kya as the content question word 'what'
kya in first position turning a statement into a yes/no question
points.note: The kya lesson teaches only the 'what' sense. Mock 1 listening item 12 and mock 2 reading item 14 both open with the polar kya, and it is the ordinary way an A1 speaking interlocutor asks anything.

points.label: kaun for a person
kahan for a place
kaise / kaisa for manner and condition
kitna / kitne for quantity
kab for time
points.note: Named in passing in the kya lesson's list of k- words, but never introduced as a word a learner can use. Mock 1 listening item 11 ('bas kab aegi?') and mock 2 item 8 ('ap kab aengi?') both ask it, and the A1 speaking role-play requires asking when a train leaves.

points.label: kyon for reason
points.note: Same status as kab: listed in the kya lesson's etymology table, never taught. Mock 2's writing task requires saying why you cannot meet.

points.label: a question word sits in the clause's normal slot rather than being fronted
points.note: The deixis-system lesson generalises the k- shape but says nothing about where the question word goes. No atom states the word-order rule.

points.label: nahin as the bare answer 'no'
ji han and ji nahin as the courteous answers
contrasting two alternatives negatively (X se nahin, Y se)
points.note: Mock 2 reading item 13 is 'main bas se nahin, train se jaunga'. Needs se, which is untaught.

points.label: the copular sentence: X Y hai
the verb comes last
points.note: Every taught sentence is verb-final, so the learner sees the order constantly, but no atom states it. A probe must point at a claim the corpus makes, not at a pattern a reader might induce.

points.label: joining two clauses with aur
points.note: aur carries a clause join in five of the six mock profile texts. It is never introduced.

points.label: closing a written sentence with the danda
points.note: HI-W06-name-sentence-stop teaches exactly this and declares an EMPTY introduces list, so it contributes no atom and cannot be probed. The gap is in the lesson's knowledge contract, not in the teaching: fixing this one frontmatter field would make the point measurable.

points.label: producing a connected two-sentence message for a named reader
points.note: HI-W06-two-sentence-card and HI-W06-two-sentence-no-model teach it and, like HI-A1-S-04, declare empty introduces lists. The A1 writing paper's second task -- 30 to 40 words to a named reader, worth 60 of that paper's 100 points -- rests on this rung.

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the numerals one to ten

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the irregular numerals eleven to twenty

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the numerals twenty-one to one hundred
points.note: The corpus stops at bis. Mock 2 reading item 4 prices tea at pachas rupaye, and no price, age over twenty, or house number can be read or said.

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the Devanagari digits 0-9 as written on signs and forms
points.note: No atom introduces the Devanagari digit shapes. Both mocks' form-reading parts render times and quantities in words, which conceals the gap rather than closing it.

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the days of the week

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the months of the year

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the parts of the day: subah, dopahar, sham, rat

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: telling the hour with bajna (ek baj raha hai)

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: naming a clock time as an appointment: X baje
points.note: The hour lesson teaches the predicate 'ek baj raha hai' -- it is one o'clock -- but not the adverbial baje that both mocks use throughout ('panch baje aunga', 'nau baje shuru hoga', 'sat baje uthti hun', 'char baje'). Reading the hour is taught; arranging to meet at it is not.

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: kal for both yesterday and tomorrow, and parson

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: abhi, ab, jaldi as points and speeds on the day

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: giving and asking an age

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: the seasons

points.category: Sankhya aur samay (numbers, time and date)
points.label: writing today's date
points.note: Mock 1's writing paper requires 'aj ki tarikh' as one of six form fields worth 16 of that task's 40 content points. Neither tarikh nor a date format is taught, and the numerals above twenty needed to write one are absent too.

points.label: the shirorekha head-line letters hang from
the abugida principle: a bare consonant already carries the inherent a
matras replace the inherent vowel
the i-matra is written before the consonant it is pronounced after
the virama stops a consonant's vowel
conjunct consonants fuse a vowel-less consonant with the next
the nasalisation marks: candrabindu, and the anusvara it is confused with
word-final schwa is written and not said
the aspirated letters are distinct from their plain twins (bha/ba, kha/ka, dha/da)
a retroflex consonant is a different letter from its dental partner
the independent vowel letters a, aa and ii, for words that begin with a vowel
the remaining independent vowels: i, u, uu, e, ai, o, au
points.note: Only a, aa and ii have atoms. Seven of the ten independent vowel letters are untaught, and A1 reading is unromanized by the track's own rule.

points.label: the matras aa, i, ii, u, e and ai
the remaining matras: uu, o, au and the vocalic ri
points.note: No atom introduces them, so a word as ordinary as 'do' or 'kaun' cannot be decoded from taught pieces.

points.label: the full consonant series, ka-varga through pa-varga and the semivowels and sibilants
points.note: The track has letter atoms for eighteen consonants (na ma ka ta ra sa pa ha ya ca sa-ssa la kha da dha bha ba da-retroflex). Fifteen more that ordinary A1 text needs -- ga gha cha ja jha ta-retroflex tha-retroflex dha-retroflex na-retroflex tha pha ba-plain va sha -- have none. Since the A1 reading paper forbids romanization, the letters with no atom are a hard ceiling on it, not a stylistic gap.

points.label: the nuqta letters qa, kha, ga, za, fa and the flapped ra, rha
points.note: The single sharpest finding in this file. The corpus's own headwords are FULL of nuqta: shukriya, khushi, zarur, safed, darvaza, mez, sabzi, zyada, safar, tohfa, bukhar, fasal, khushbu, mulaqat. Learners are shown the letters constantly and never taught the mark, so no atom can be probed for it.

points.label: writing a complete known sentence, with word spacing
completing a form field in Devanagari with no visible model
completing every field of an A1 practical form (name, city, language, time, drink, date)
points.note: The form rung proves exactly one field, the name. Both mocks' writing task 1 asks for six, and the rubric gives a blank field no content point.

points.label: the aspirated/unaspirated contrast changes the word
the retroflex/dental contrast changes the word
nasalised vowels
long and short vowels are different vowels
the borrowed consonants z, f and q as sounds, not just as spellings
points.note: The corpus teaches the words that carry them and never the sounds. See HI-A1-SCR-16, its written twin.

points.label: rising intonation marks a yes/no question when no kya is present
points.note: No atom addresses intonation. The A1 listening paper plays every exchange as speech, and the polar questions in it are carried by intonation as often as by kya.

points.label: word stress and the rhythm of a phrase
points.note: Untreated in the corpus. Recorded at A1 for the same reason the Spanish inventory records its pronunciation gap: no source draws an A1/A2 line for it, so the point is enumerated and left honestly unmapped.

points.label: greet at any hour with namaste, and choose namaskar when the setting is formal
greet in the morning
greet in the afternoon
greet in the evening
wish someone good night
judge which greeting register a situation wants
take leave, formally and casually
say you will see someone tomorrow
thank someone, choosing between the Sanskritic and the everyday word
answer thanks
apologise
say please in writing and on a sign
make a spoken request across a counter with the -iye form
give your name
ask someone's name
say you are pleased to meet someone
ask how someone is
say how you are
say which language you speak
say where you live
ask where someone is from, and say where you are from
points.note: The first question of the A1 speaking interview and of mock 1 listening item 10. It needs se, which is untaught. See HI-A1-POST-04.

points.label: say what work you do
give your age
answer a question yes or no
say what you like
order a drink
ask what something costs
points.note: Required by mock 1's speaking role-play part 3, which is 40 of that paper's 100 points. Needs kitne ka, rupaye, and numerals above twenty -- none of which the corpus has.

points.label: say what you need
points.note: Needs chahiye. See HI-A1-V-16.

points.label: ask when something happens
points.note: Needs kab. See HI-A1-Q-07.

points.label: propose meeting again
propose a specific day, time and place to meet
points.note: The writing task in BOTH mocks ends on it. kal milte hain proposes a day and nothing else; the time needs baje (HI-A1-NUM-09) and the place needs par or me with a place noun the corpus does not have.

points.label: decline, and say why you cannot
points.note: Mock 2's writing task opens on it. Needs kyon and a negated modal.

points.label: say you did not understand, and ask for a repetition
points.note: samajhna is taught as a dictionary verb; no atom builds the repair move, and the A1 speaking construct scores interaction and repair at 25 percent of every part.

points.label: describe the weather
describe a daily routine
points.note: The one-minute prepared description and the personal-account listening part in both mocks are routines. The habitual tense is taught, but jana, uthna, baje, se and par -- everything a routine is made of besides the tense -- are not.

points.label: ask for help
welcome someone
point at a thing and ask what it is
read a public sign: entrance, exit, open, closed
points.note: Items 1 to 4 of BOTH mocks' reading papers, and the first 35 of that paper's 100 points. The corpus introduces no sign vocabulary at all -- not pravesh, nikas, band, khula, bahar, or dhyan den.

points.label: read a practical form's field labels and say which field holds what
personal identity: name and age
the family
people and social roles
the body
the house and its parts
furniture and household objects
food and drink
kitchen staples
animals
colours
the sky and the natural world
weather words
places in a town
school and study
work
everyday action verbs
verbs of the mind
bodily states: hunger, thirst, sleep, fever, pain
courtesy nouns
adverbs of manner and degree
short response words: sac, bas, zarur, shayad, bilkul
transport: bas, tren, saikil, station, gari
points.note: Both mocks' reading, listening and speaking papers ask about transport, and the A1 speaking interview lists it as one of five interview topics. The corpus has safar ('a journey') and nothing that moves.

points.label: money and shopping: rupaya, dam, kitne ka
points.note: dukan and bazar are taught as places. No unit of money, no price word, and no numeral above twenty, so the cafe role-play's price turn cannot be attempted.

points.label: naming a second language, and naming countries and nationalities
points.note: hindi is taught inside 'main hindi bolta hun'. angrezi is not, and neither is bharat or any country name -- yet mock 1 item 16 and mock 2 item 20 both key on someone speaking TWO languages, and 'bhasha' is a form field in both writing papers.

points.label: the words a town sign or a station announcement uses
points.note: The lexical twin of HI-A1-F-39. dhyan den, shuru, taiyar, der se, khula, band, pravesh, nikas, platform: none is introduced, and they carry the opening items of both papers that are scored first.
